summary:
Galicia stands under Spain's Ley 4/2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 28 February 2023 (BOE-A-2023-5366), on real and effective equality for trans persons and the guarantee of LGBTI rights. Title II of the law regulates rectification of the registered sex entry by the person's freely expressed will. The procedure is depathologised: no medical diagnosis or treatment is required, the former age-majority requirement for filing has been removed, and identity documents are adapted accordingly.

Article 43 of Ley 4/2023 allows any person aged 16 or over to request rectification directly before the Civil Registry. Recognition is available from age 12 under stated conditions, a provision that provoked political conflict when the law was passed. Title III provides protection and reparation against LGBTIphobic discrimination and violence, and the law mandates measures across administrative, workplace, health and education fields, with public authorities acting within their competences. The education-facing and administrative provisions are implemented by the autonomous communities, the Xunta de Galicia among them.

Human Rights Watch, writing on 16 February 2023 as the Congress of Deputies passed the law, described legal gender recognition by self-identification through a simple administrative process, replacing the prior requirements of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment aligned to the sought marker. The same law bans medically unnecessary normalising surgery on intersex children before they can consent, enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, prohibits LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing, and strengthens sexuality education. Human Rights Watch assesses the reform as upholding European and international standards against abusive, disproportionate requirements for legal gender recognition.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules in Galicia.

Transphobic motivation is an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code, and the hate-speech provision at Article 510 carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months. Both derive from Organic Law 6/2022 rather than from Ley 4/2023. Gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code, so a hate crime grounded in gender expression has no free-standing offence; Ley 4/2023 instead reformed the offences against sexual freedom at Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Courts apply the aggravation in practice. In Vigo, a Tribunal de Instancia used the transfobia aggravation for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300. In Valencia, a juvenile gang that harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park produced a six-month prison sentence for the only adult defendant, while two minors were judged separately.

Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have applied in Spain since 2005, and the country is ranked comparatively among the most LGBT-friendly in the world.
tangentialFactors:
Ley 4/2023 was not the source of the hate-crime machinery a visitor may rely on. The aggravating circumstance at Article 22.4 and the hate-speech offence at Article 510 both predate it, arriving with Organic Law 6/2022, so protection against transphobic violence rests on the Criminal Code as reformed in 2022 rather than on the 2023 equality statute.

Because gender expression is not named anywhere in the Criminal Code, an assault motivated by how a person presents rather than by their legal status has no separate offence to charge, and prosecutors must route such conduct through the general offences. Ley 4/2023's own penal contribution concerns offences against sexual freedom at Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

The intersex surgery ban, the extension of parental recognition to unmarried same-sex couples, and the sexuality-education measures all sit inside the same statute as gender recognition. They indicate the breadth of the law rather than changing what a trans visitor must do on arrival.

Spain's comparatively favourable ranking on LGBT friendliness, and the 2005 extension of marriage and adoption to same-sex couples, sit alongside a documented record of transphobic violence, including the park assault in Valencia. A high-level national ranking does not by itself describe what happens on the street.
localsOnly:
The Xunta de Galicia carries the implementation of the education-facing and administrative provisions of Ley 4/2023 within its competences, alongside the general mandate covering workplace, health and administrative fields.

Residents file for rectification of the registered sex entry directly before the Civil Registry by their freely expressed will, with no diagnosis, no treatment requirement and no age-majority threshold on the request itself; those aged 16 and over act on their own, and recognition is available from age 12 under the conditions set in the law. Identity documents are adapted to the rectified entry.

Protection and reparation against LGBTIphobic discrimination and violence under Title III is available to residents, and the aggravating circumstance at Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code operates at sentencing when transphobic motivation is proved.

Unmarried same-sex couples may obtain parental recognition, and same-sex couples have had full marriage and adoption rights since 2005.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether any Galician court besides the Vigo Tribunal de Instancia has applied the transfobia aggravation is not sourced here; the Vigo case is presented as the first use, and the Valencia case sits outside this autonomous community.

The enforcement record for the facility-access rule and for the intersex surgery ban in Galicia specifically is not resolved by the available inventory, which speaks to the national framework rather than to regional practice.

The penalties for physically assaulting a trans person on the basis of gender identity, as distinct from the hate-speech range at Article 510 and the six-month Valencia sentence, are not stated in the sources and are left unresolved.

How the age-12 recognition conditions are applied in practice, and which authority in Galicia decides them, is not sourced; the inventory records only that recognition is possible from 12 under conditions and that the provision drew political conflict.
